title: Burnham says he is prepared to call out Trump 'if right for Britain'
description: Image caption, Andy Burnham spoke exclusively to Laura Kuenssberg this week in his first major interview as prime minister BySunday with Laura Kuenssb
body: Image caption, Andy Burnham spoke exclusively to Laura Kuenssberg this week in his first major interview as prime minister BySunday with Laura KuenssbergAndy Burnham says he would be prepared to call out Donald Trump to defend Britain's "national interest before anything else" if it is the right thing to do, in his first major interview as prime minister.Speaking exclusively to the BBC, Burnham said he had had a good first exchange with Trump, finding him to be "really warm".But asked twice if he would trust the US president, he did not say, answering, "it's a changing world isn't it, and you just obviously have to call things as they develop".In the interview, to be broadcast in full on Monday, he said: "I can't at any point say that I won't take a different opinion from him [Trump], that I will need to voice a different idea that is right for Britain."Figure caption, Watch: 'You have to defend your own national interest before anything else'Burnham said: "My strength is remaining close to people, close to the public, that will not change as prime minister."Asked if he would call out Trump if it was the right thing, he said, "of course", going on to say: "You have to defend your own national interest before anything else. That's what you're required to do if you're to do this job properly."Burnham also said he had had "concern" about the president starting the conflict with Iran, and he "wouldn't hold back from saying what I think is right".The prime minister would not commit to a date when the government would spend 3% of GDP on defence. His Chancellor John Healey resigned from the previous government saying that unless a commitment was made to spend that amount by 2030, the country would not be safe.But Burnham said: "I appointed my new chancellor very aware of what he had said about the critical importance of defence spending and the position that he had taken about that."The first challenge facing us both is to ensure that the defence investment plan is fully funded and that's the thing that's right in front of us and we need to work that through as we go towards the budget later this year."Figure caption, Watch: PM says 'we've got to work out the way' of meeting defence promisesAsked again specifically about the commitment to increase defence spending to 3% of GDP, he said: "We've got to work out the way of doing that."Burnham, for the first time, explicitly dismissed the idea of an early general election before 2029, saying: "I'm going to rule it out... I don't think people want it." He said his focus instead was on "getting the country back where it should be".Watch the full interview, BBC Panorama 'Andy Burnham: the Laura Kuenssberg Interview' on iPlayer from 06:00 on Monday and BBC One on Monday at 20:00 BST.

schema.headline: Burnham says he is prepared to call out Trump 'if right for Britain'

title: Wes Streeting: UK not intimidated by Iran's 'sabre rattling'
description: When asked if Iran had the capability to attack the UK, Streeting said: "I think we shouldn't put too much stock in the sabre-rattling of Iran, and we
body: When asked if Iran had the capability to attack the UK, Streeting said: "I think we shouldn't put too much stock in the sabre-rattling of Iran, and we certainly shouldn't be intimidated by what the regime has said this week".He also repeated the UK's position from the outset of the US war against Iran saying "we have not joined and will not join offensive US military action in Iran. "That's an area where we have not agreed with the United States, but when it comes to securing maritime freedom and free commercial shipping in the straight Hormuz, that's where we are absolutely aligned".Streeting said he is to meet with US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth in the coming week after "kicking around" ideas for ways "to bring the countries together" and had been "delighted" to speak to Hegseth by phone already.He also said that the UK is ready to lead a naval mission to help remove mines from the Strait of Hormuz "when the conditions are right".Securing safe shipping routes through the area was important because of the impact the crisis is having on energy prices and the cost of living, he added.Streeting also dismissed a Russian warship's recent live-firing exercise in the English Channel as "performative" but added it was a "reminder of the frankly unsafe and unprofessional way in which they have been conducting themselves".Branding the Channel incident "irresponsible", Streeting said Russia posed a threat to UK security, adding that the public does not see "the enormous efforts that take place every day to counter Russian aggression".

schema.headline: Wes Streeting: UK not intimidated by Iran's 'sabre rattling'

title: Commonwealth Games 2026: Adam Ramsay-Peaty in tears after bronze medal
description: After tears in Paris, tears again in Glasgow.It leaves even the great Adam Ramsay-Peaty wondering how much of this is worth it."I work a lot harder th
body: After tears in Paris, tears again in Glasgow.It leaves even the great Adam Ramsay-Peaty wondering how much of this is worth it."I work a lot harder than what it says on the scoreboard," the Englishman said after taking 100m breaststroke bronze at the Commonwealth Games, his eyes and cheeks red with emotion."It hurts too much. I have got to approach training differently now because it hurts too much."Ramsay-Peaty has done it all in this sport.Three Olympic gold medals. Eight world titles. The 14 fastest times in history.But after taking a break from swimming amid a wave of mental health issues in 2023, he is still searching for that winning feeling again on the big stage.He was pipped to Olympic gold in Paris two years ago. In Glasgow, despite coming into the final as the fastest qualifier, he had to settle for bronze.He was beaten by Australia's Sam Williamson but also Jersey's history-maker Filip Nowacki, the 18-year-old he has taken under his wing.Ramsay-Peaty was third at halfway and could not close the gap. His time - 59.65 seconds - was more than four-tenths slower than his semi-final swim and three seconds off his personal best from seven years ago."It took a lot of courage to get back into the sport, so we should be happy with everything we get, but then that contradicts the athlete inside me and what I work for," he said."I just think I deserve more. I know sport isn't about what you deserve or even what you work for - it's who gets it on the day."I just know I'm a better athlete than that. It's very disappointing."Ramsay-Peaty has spoken about the difficult decisions that come with being an elite athlete. The time away from his son, whom he held in his arms after the Paris silver. The events at home he has to miss."They are not even sacrifices; they are choices," he said."It's like getting knocked out in the group stages in the World Cup for a very good team. You know you're better and it hurts because you know you have to wait for a very long time for the next championships."This is probably - realistically - my last Commonwealth Games and I thought I'd trained for better. I could do better. I've been faster this season. That's where the frustration is."Ramsay-Peaty has made no secret of the fact he is still competing in the quest for Olympic gold.He considered retirement again after Paris, but committed to another four years when the 50m race was added to programme for Los Angeles 2028.This 100m breaststroke is his event - the one in which he went unbeaten in eight years - but there may be a time when he has to let it go.The 50m race - a dash down one length of the pool - would be less taxing on the body, and Ramsay-Peaty is due back in the pool for that event on Sunday morning."Is the 100 even viable any more? I don't know," he said."When it hurts like this, the 50 is probably my super strength with my power."With the Olympics, that's probably going to be more realistic, but it's too early to tell."I just feel like I couldn't have given more this cycle. If I had given less, would it have even equalled more?"Given the emotion, there are times you wonder how close Ramsay-Peaty is to walking away entirely.He  appeared to walk to the edge but always turned back, insisting the drive for LA remains."Of course," he said."I know I'm a sprinter. I know I can do very well because I've done it. It doesn't disappear overnight."It requires me to look at the formula and see how I can get to that speed again."

schema.headline: Commonwealth Games 2026: Adam Ramsay-Peaty in tears after bronze medal

title: Aitch on reaching new heights with his Mount Kilimanjaro climb
description: How rapper Aitch's sister inspired him to climb one of the world's toughest peaksImage source, Aaron FitzmauriceImage caption, The Manchester rapper h
body: How rapper Aitch's sister inspired him to climb one of the world's toughest peaksImage source, Aaron FitzmauriceImage caption, The Manchester rapper has been pursuing challenges to raise awareness and money for the Down's Syndrome AssociationByEleanor Doyle and Naomi ClarkeBBC NewsbeatHe's skydived, eaten raw fish eyes on I'm a Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here! and now Aitch has reached new heights - literally - by climbing Mount Kilimanjaro.The Manchester rapper has been pursuing some of these tasks to raise awareness and money for the Down's Syndrome Association in honour of his younger sister Gracie, who has the condition. Aitch tells BBC Newsbeat the 16-year-old is an "absolute legend in the streets of Manchester" and beyond."Everyone loves her. She's just a big bottle of light in every room," he says."She's everyone's best friend and she's just got such a positive outlook on the world. "I just feel like everyone should be more like her."The musician's journey up Kilimanjaro has been captured in an upcoming Netflix documentary, Aitch: Don't Be Afraid.But he says the whole point of it was to share how having someone in his life with Down's syndrome is "one of the best things in the world".However, the 26-year-old admits he does feel "a little bit of pressure" to up the scale and fundraising targets of his challenges."You've just got to think about the end goal, which is trying to raise the most money and make the most difference to what's going on," he says.Image source, HandoutImage caption, Aitch says his sister Gracie is an "absolute legend in the streets of Manchester" and beyondHe has "smashed" his target this time by bringing in more than £160,000 so far from his climb of the highest peak in Africa. The rapper says he was able to handle the altitude and physical elements of the hike, which others in his group struggled with. But the "big mental challenge" was the biggest obstacle for him, he says.Between the early mornings, late nights and the change of climate from rainforest conditions one minute to a blizzard the next, Aitch says it was "just all a lot".He confesses the group would probably have turned around if they hadn't been doing the climb for "such a good cause".Down's syndrome is when you're born with an extra chromosome - and people with the condition are likely to have some level of learning disability.Aitch's fundraising efforts have been inspired by Gracie, who was also the subject of My G, a viral song he released in 2022. He thinks it was so popular because it showed the bond between the siblings."People love genuine things," he says."And that relationship there between me and my sister, both of my sisters, is just undeniable. Do you know what I'm saying? So I feel like that's why people loved it."Image source, Down’s Syndrome AssociationImage caption, The rapper's fundraising efforts have been inspired by Gracie, who was also the subject of his viral song My GHaving grown up as a sibling carer, Aitch has faced challenges, and seen Gracie overcome obstacles. Reflecting on how he would advise others in his position who are struggling, he says  "you've got to see the blessing in it every time". "I suppose if you ask yourself the question, 'would you change it for the world?', there's probably not a chance," he says."So it's always going to be a bit of a challenge, but sometimes you've got to just take it on the chin, keep it stepping and it'll all be all right."He also feels there is "always more that can be done" to support young carers and  improve understanding around various conditions and learning disabilities. "Where I stand, I'm trying to do what I do to raise awareness," he says. "And hopefully that brings people in. "Hopefully that makes people want to get a little bit more involved in the whole thing and just spread more awareness than ever." Aitch: Don't Be Afraid is available to stream on Netflix from 26 July. Listen to Newsbeat live at 12:45 and 17:45 weekdays - or listen back here.

schema.headline: Aitch on reaching new heights with his Mount Kilimanjaro climb

title: Your tips on getting a fussy child to eat, and six recipes they'll love
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByPhilippa RoxbyHealth reporterIt's the start of the summer holidays and you've already had five battles with your child to
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByPhilippa RoxbyHealth reporterIt's the start of the summer holidays and you've already had five battles with your child to get them to eat a bit of broccoli. For many parents, these few weeks can be a stressful time of the year at the dinner table. So how should we deal with our picky eaters? The BBC asked you for your tips on making mealtimes a more enjoyable experience.Encourage eating veg by changing how you serve themMum-of-four Natalia, from south-west London, makes veggie nuggets for her children."They like green beans but not by themselves, so we just fry them in a little bit of butter and dip in breadcrumbs. The same with cauliflower and lots of other vegetables," she says.Teacher Kieron Fisher, who lives in Newbury, Berkshire, includes vegetables in meals his six-year-old twins Kit and Ollie already enjoy, such as curries and spaghetti Bolognese."It helps increase their vegetable intake without causing a battle."Image source, Kieron FisherImage caption, Kieron's twins Kit and Ollie can be "quite fussy at times" but picnicking in the park is always a hitEmma Robins, from Reading, says broccoli hidden in pesto pasta is a favourite for her three-year-old son Alfred, as well as veg pulsed into pasta sauces. She also recommends making your own burgers with vegetables.A lack of routine in the holidays can be particularly challenging for some children, so Kieron suggests using visual boards showing the healthy snack they are about to have and another showing the activity they are going to do next.Children with special educational needs can sometimes experience sensory difficulties when it comes to food - and are not classified as fussy eaters. Some of these suggestions may not be suitable for them.Don't force them to finish everything on their plate"If they're hungry, they'll eat. I don't force them to because I think that can instil pressure," says Doone, from London. She says her daughter Cora, two, used to be the "best eater" but seeing others at nursery turn their noses up at certain foods made her do the same."I'm trying not to make a big deal of it. Even though they don't eat it, I always put the broccoli on the plate so that they're seeing it."Emma suggests giving lots of options, so that kids think they are getting to choose. In Alfred's lunchbox, she always adds two or three healthy options.And she says to praise them when they take an interest. "If they say one day they want carrots, run and get the carrots and give big praise when they eat them," Emma says.Keep offering food until they try it  It may take up to 15 attempts before kids learn to like new foods, research suggests."Keep going," says one mum outside Barnes Primary School, in south-west London. "Keep offering it and they will pick it up and try it. We try to make everyone try everything in our house, even the tiniest bit."Sometimes it can be the colour or texture of a certain food that puts them off, another parent says, until they actually try it.Children refusing to eat new foods or rejecting ones they've always liked is not unusual. More than half will show fussy eating habits at some point, the NHS says, external.Vegetables, in particular, can taste quite bitter to young palates. Most habits will improve over time.But if your kids start to avoid certain foods and limit how much they eat in an unhealthy way, it's worth seeking medical advice, external.Make eating a family affair - and get the portion size right"I always eat with my girls and I eat what they're eating," says Doone, who has two "quite fussy eaters".The British Nutrition Foundation agrees that food should be a family affair - allowing children to learn from what their parents do. When a bit older, they can help with preparation too.Emma adds to the fun by taking her kids fruit picking and also by letting them choose at the supermarket, then having tasty picnics in the garden.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Nutritionists says food should be a family affair - allowing children to learn from what their parents doBut first thing's first, says Kieron: think about the portion size."I make sure their plates aren't too full or overcrowded, as too much food at once can feel overwhelming," he says.Serve snacks alongside healthier options Doone says: "I am making a conscious effort not to give many snacks because then they're more hungry at dinner time."Natalia leaves out healthy finger food, like chopped peppers and apples, for her children to pick at.Image caption, Finger food is easy to pick at Don't completely ban them, says Kieron - just serve snacks alongside healthier options, like berries or other fruit, replicate snack times at school and don't stress about the odd treat."Six weeks [of summer holidays] is a long time, so it's about focusing on the overall balance of their diet rather than aiming for perfection every day," he says.

schema.headline: Your tips on getting a fussy child to eat, and six recipes they'll love

title: Joshua vs Fury: Where does AJ's 'chaotic' win in Saudi Arabia leave heavyweight blockbuster?
description: In the aftermath of such a chaotic night, it is easy to focus only on the flaws and forget the bigger picture. Joshua was returning from one of the da
body: In the aftermath of such a chaotic night, it is easy to focus only on the flaws and forget the bigger picture. Joshua was returning from one of the darkest periods of his life and carrying an immense emotional burden into the ring.After his hand was raised, he struggled to get through his interview. His voice cracked as he spoke about his two friends and the impact their loss has had on him."Boxing once saved him and he needed boxing to get through this. That camp allowed him to focus his mind while he was in so much grief and pain," promoter Eddie Hearn said."You don't know what he was going through in that camp because he doesn't talk about it."Whatever happens next, his place in British boxing history is already secure. He is an Olympic gold medallist, a two-time heavyweight champion and one of the biggest sporting stars this country has produced.He has taken boxing to places few British fighters ever have. He has filled stadiums, headlined global events and become a household name far beyond the sport.But in the build-up to his comeback, Joshua and his stablemate Oleksandr Usyk spoke about the ambition of becoming undisputed heavyweight champion.After Saturday night in Saudi, the reality is that even reclaiming a world title would be a tough ask.Joshua has always spoken about legacy, and there would be something fitting about walking away after overcoming one of the toughest periods of his life and producing a dramatic comeback victory.The danger with ageing fighters is chasing one more night. Boxing history is filled with champions who stayed that one fight too long.But then again Fury-Joshua is not one more fight. It is the fight. The one that has loomed over their careers for the best part of a decade.

schema.headline: Joshua vs Fury: Where does AJ's 'chaotic' win in Saudi Arabia leave heavyweight blockbuster?

title: Liverpool: Joe Gomez injury overshadows winning start for Andoni Iraola
description: Liverpool started life under Andoni Iraola with a 4-2 win over Sunderland thanks to goals from Kieran Morrison, Dominik Szoboszlai, Federico Chiesa an
body: Liverpool started life under Andoni Iraola with a 4-2 win over Sunderland thanks to goals from Kieran Morrison, Dominik Szoboszlai, Federico Chiesa and Lewis Koumas. But the Iraola era had initially got off to the worst possible start when Joe Gomez, who started the game as centre-back and captain, went down injured and was taken off in the eighth minute."Probably the worst news has been straight away the injury of Joe. We were happy because we were going through training without losing any players and unluckily for us we've lost Joe straight away," said Iraola, who was also without new signing Jeremy Jacquet - who plays centre-half - for the opening friendly of Liverpool's tour of the USA."With Jeremy we decided to take it easy with him. He's had a lot of months without playing and he's been training very well but we're going to take it easy with him," Iraola added. "He will play probably in the last game of this tour and he will have time to have minutes."With Virgil van Dijk given extra time off following the Netherlands' World Cup campaign, it meant that two teenage centre-backs held the line until the 68th minute.Mor Talla N'diaye, 18, and Ifeanyi Ndukwe, 18, made their debuts and both performed admirably given the situation but neither can be expected to feature regularly yet. Meanwhile, Giovanni Leoni, 19, is still undergoing individual training as he works his way back from a severe ACL tear. Iraola said earlier in the week that his squad was "very thin" defensively. Liverpool's sporting director, Richard Hughes, was in Nashville for the game and if he wasn't aware already, seeing Gomez trudge off must have underlined how they are desperately short when it comes to experience in the centre-back department.On Friday evening, some of the Liverpool squad took the short walk from their hotel in downtown Nashville to Broadway - the famous entertainment district here in the state of Tennessee.Szoboszlai, who was among that group, certainly took some inspiration. Wearing the armband after coming on at half-time and picking up from exactly where he left off last season, the Hungarian scored a belter from outside the box to level the game at 2-2 after Sunderland had gone ahead through Timur Tutierov, having initially levelled through Enzo le Fee.Seeing Harvey Elliott make a surging run on his first game back at the club, after his spell at Aston Villa, to assist Morrison for Liverpool's opener was another positive.  Morrison, 19, showed his quality with a lovely left-footed finish after cutting in from the right. The 19-year-old Northern Ireland international was brilliant all evening and asked plenty of questions of the Sunderland backline. Liverpool still need a quality winger after losing Mohamed Salah but Morrison showed why he could be an option off the bench if he doesn't go out on loan this summer.Iraola was constantly out of his seat in the dugout and his side pressed well in phases but the manner in which they conceded both goals shows there is still plenty to be done. Le Fee was given the freedom of Nashville to fire his strike past Giorgi Mamardashvili and Liverpool were opened up far too easy for Tutierov's goal.For the 24,897 fans inside, who were primarily following Liverpool, it provided great joy to see fan favourite Chiesa make it 3-2, with a brilliant finish after a good ball from Calvin Ramsay, before Koumas capped off an impressive display with a goal to wrap up the game.Earlier on in that move, Josh Abe played an important role carrying the ball up the pitch down the right flank. Abe only turned 16 last week and came on for his Liverpool debut in the second half. The England youth international is a highly rated prospect and there were glimpses here of why.Iraola and co head back to their base in Chicago with a win under their belt but well aware that this is just the start. Florian Wirtz, Alexander Isak and Ryan Gravenberch have already arrived in the Windy City and start training on Sunday."It doesn't matter the result but keep pushing, don't relax, get used to not playing too comfortable. We still have a lot of things to improve," the Liverpool head coach said. His side are next in action against Wrexham in New York on Thursday (00.30 BST). Sunderland face Leeds at the Sports Illustrated Stadium in New Jersey at the same time.

schema.headline: Liverpool: Joe Gomez injury overshadows winning start for Andoni Iraola

title: France battles fire 'whirlwinds' as another 55,000 evacuated
description: A further 55,000 people have been evacuated from six towns in France, as wildfires which have caused devastation across the country pick up pace. The
body: A further 55,000 people have been evacuated from six towns in France, as wildfires which have caused devastation across the country pick up pace. The most recent evacuations took place in towns to the south of Bordeaux, in the Gironde region. Wildfires have raged across Europe over the past week, primarily France and Spain, where more than 330,000 people have been evacuated. France has been worst-affected, with an area of 42,000 hectares burnt, making it one of the largest forest fires since World War Two. About 98,000 hectares have burnt across the country since the start of the year. Captain Nicolas Braz, one of the leaders of the firefighting operation, said the fire had created "its own winds - complete with whirlwinds", adding it was "erratic and unmanageable".France's Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said on Sunday the situation in the region remained "very unfavourable" and the wildfire was "moving erratically towards the Bordeaux metropolitan area".Dry vegetation and brisk winds are causing the fire to spread, with 60km (37 miles) of the A63 motorway, which leads to Spain, having been closed. In an interview published on Sunday by La Tribune, Nunez said it "will take a long time to bring under control" and until it is contained "there will be no return" for evacuated residents and tourists. France has mobilised its military to help with the response and extra reinforcements from the army have been sent to help firefighters by clearing brush and creating fire breaks.President Emmanuel Macron said France would "rebuild" and his government would "be there for as long as is needed".Meanwhile in Spain, fires continue to spread, with more than 90,000 evacuated from the regions around Madrid and Ávila.Late on Saturday, at least eight municipalities near Toledo were also ordered to evacuate, though it was unclear how many people were involved.Sunday is expected to bring high temperatures and low humidity, potentially allowing the fire to spread further. Madrid's regional president Isabel Díaz Ayuso described the situation as the "worst fire in the history of the region".Spanish PM Pedro Sánchez admitted there were "complex times ahead". Meanwhile, authorities in València confirmed the death of a man in a fire.

schema.headline: France battles fire 'whirlwinds' as another 55,000 evacuated

title: Primark cuts prices as it feels pressure from Shein and Temu
description: "Primark isn't as cheap any more."It is something I keep hearing shoppers say when I ask them whether they shop at the fast-fashion giant."It's defini
body: "Primark isn't as cheap any more."It is something I keep hearing shoppers say when I ask them whether they shop at the fast-fashion giant."It's definitely got more expensive," says 19-year-old student Eshal Malik as she browses the jewellery at Primark with a friend.But that might be about to change. Primark said on Monday that it was lowering prices on hundreds of clothing items, including jeans, jumpers and socks."It's the kind of headline you'd expect from M&S or Next," says retail analyst Natalie Berg, explaining that price cuts like this from such a low-cost retailer are surprising."You don't want to join a race to the bottom," she says. "But when Shein is selling dresses for £3, you've got to respond, right?"Primark, which has more than 190 UK stores, has been experiencing a drop in like-for-like sales, a key measure in the retail industry. The announcement of price cuts comes ahead of parent company Associated British Foods' plan to spin off the business onto the London stock market next year.The level of competition among fashion retailers has "evolved dramatically" over the past few years, and Chinese online marketplaces Shein and Temu are now competing for Primark's customers, says Berg.But there is also competition from other online retailers like TikTok Shop and Vinted, she says.By slashing prices on some core items, Primark is likely hoping to woo shoppers with low-cost staples, in the same way that supermarkets attract customers with cheap milk and bananas, Berg says.Temu and Shein have been able to undercut traditional retailers like Primark because they do not pay for physical locations, most of their packages are exempt from import duties – though this exemption is set to end in October 2028, external - and they have an efficient operating model that leaves them with little unsold stock, says Berg.Currently low Shein prices are seen as the new baseline, Berg says. And they are luring in younger shoppers. According to Mintel research from July 2025, 32% of women aged 16-34 who buy clothes online said they had shopped at Shein during the previous year. Low prices, abundant discount codes and seemingly endless pages of products all feed into its attraction.Primark, in contrast, has a click and collect service but does not offer delivery.Some shoppers think better value for money can be found elsewhere on the High Street.Isobel Guffick, 30, from Staffordshire, feels Sainsbury's Tu range has greater quality clothes for similar prices. It is "really good for basics", she says.To save money, she also buys clothes secondhand where possible, from charity shops, car boot sales and sites like Vinted. She visits charity shops every week and loves the "treasure hunt" feel of finding a bargain.Getting a couple of pounds off a jumper or a pair of jeans might not seem like a lot to a customer, but for a shop with tight margins like Primark, how might this affect the business?"Our business model and focus on buying at scale and keeping costs low helps us to offer the prices we do, but we don't compromise on quality or ethics to do that," a Primark spokesperson told BBC News. In its latest annual report, it said that about 85% of its products are £10 or less.Crucially, the new lower prices do not cover everything Primark sells. McCusker describes the price reductions as a marketing exercise designed to bring in more shoppers - and says that even if they are drawn in by the lower prices of jeans or jumpers, they'll probably end up putting other items in their basket, too."Primark is known for that impulse nature," she explains.One big issue for some fashion retailers is having big piles of leftover stock that has to be discounted heavily so they can shift it. Primark will be expecting that the price changes "will help them shift stock, meaning they don't have to discount too much any further," says AJ Bell analyst Russ Mould.Ultimately analysts think Primark's new pricing is in response to a highly competitive retail environment."When it comes to staying relevant to customers today, you have to offer value for money," Berg says. "Especially if you are meant to be the value fashion retailer in the UK, you have to deliver on that promise."

schema.headline: Primark cuts prices as it feels pressure from Shein and Temu

title: Jail Time Records: The notorious Cameroonian prison with its own record label
description: New Bell - a notorious prison in Douala, Cameroon - is a city within a city.The facility has its own "taxis" (inmates who whizz through congested cour
body: New Bell - a notorious prison in Douala, Cameroon - is a city within a city.The facility has its own "taxis" (inmates who whizz through congested courtyards on foot to hand deliver messages), its own law enforcement (burly prisoners who help stretched guards police the facility) and market (a string of stalls where convicts sell and buy goodies, like fried cassava and beignet pastries).Basically, the occupants of New Bell have adapted the jail's slack laws to work for them. The clearest example of this spirit is Jail Time Records, an on-site music studio and label making mini stars out of the most talented prisoners.Empereur, the feared leader of gangs inside and outside of the prison, has amassed 24,000 YouTube views with a music video filmed entirely in prison.Songs from the inmates have gained fans from as far away as South Africa, the US and Argentina, while earlier this year Jail Time Records put on a huge concert for the prisoners in New Bell's courtyard. "It's this instrument of resistance… where we can really share friendship, love and our voices can be heard," Steve Happi, the former inmate who co-founded Jail Time Records, tells the BBC's Talking Movies programme."We don't think anymore about the four walls - we find the freedom."The Jail Time Records studio is rudimentary - a small, sweaty recording booth attached to a room inhabited by a solitary computer.But it is also the site of great catharsis and creativity, as per a recent, acclaimed documentary named after the studio.Directed by Happi and Italian artist Dione Roach, his Jail Time Records co-founder, it was filmed in New Bell over six years. Last month it won three prizes, including best documentary feature, at New York's Tribeca film festival.In the film, a prisoner named Stone raps into the studio's microphone: "Heart of stone, it's war. My senses shatter like broken glass."I'm closed and tight like a cell door. No solid ground I slip like a fish."Stone, who used to be a soldier in Cameroon's presidential guard, was sentenced to 10 years in New Bell for robbery and illegal possession of firearms. He insists he is not guilty.The film captures him trying - often unsuccessfully - to reach his young daughter Maira on the phone."It's been a long time. She needs to hear my voice from time to time, so she doesn't forget about her father," he says in a voice message to a family member, after failing to get through to Maira yet again.The music video for Heart of Stone is a typical Jail Time Records affair. The production value is high, storytelling is captivating and hordes of fellow inmates get involved as actors and crew. "The music that comes out of there is amazing," says Taika Waititi, the New Zealand Oscar-winning director who, with his wife, the singer Rita Ora, served as an executive producer for the Jail Time Records documentary. "Just in terms of the power of art in relation to redemption and what that can mean to someone who, you know, some of these people are in prison for life. I think having an outlet is an incredibly powerful and humane thing," he says.Jail Time Records was founded in 2018, when Roach volunteered for a non-profit organisation running events inside New Bell. During a dance class for the prisoners, a crew of rappers took over the microphone and began freestyling. Impressed by their performance, she asked the prison authorities for permission to start up a studio.The powers that be were receptive and so Roach enlisted Happi to run the studio as a producer and sound engineer.According to Happi, he ended up in New Bell following a family argument over what should be done with his late father's body. Amid the dispute, his aunt, a high court judge, allegedly arranged for him to be thrown into jail for killing his father. He was acquitted of the crime two years later, Jail Time Records says. In 2022, Happi, Roach and the prisoners released an album named Jail Time Vol 1. As is customary for Jail Time Records' music, half the profit from the album's sale went to the artists and the rest was reinvested into the label.The studio's survival is paramount to many of the artists, especially given New Bell's bitter environment. In 2022, Human Rights Watch reported that New Bell was housing 4,700 prisoners within its crumbling walls - four times its capacity. The prison's packed population, along with its unsanitary conditions, enabled cholera to spread rapidly during an outbreak four years ago, rights groups have said. At least six inmates died from the disease.New Bell also has a reputation for violence. In 2008, guards shot 16 inmates dead during an attempted breakout.Prisoners also attack and intimidate each other - the documentary captures Empereur, who is serving 10 years for multiple crimes, shaking down a bewildered young inmate for a necklace chain and some flip-flops. Asked if the Jail Time Records project might glorify Empereur, the son of a traditional Douala chief, and other criminals who have committed violent crimes, Roach tells the BBC: "The process we're doing is a rehabilitation process, basically. "We enter the prison without any judgment and it's the only way we can really approach this kind of work."Music, as with any creative process, is also a way of self-discovery... coming to terms with things you've done and hopefully changing for the better".The prison authorities appear to share this view."They were really welcoming of the project. Cameroon is a super musical country… everyone loves music," Happi says, adding that the head of the prison attended this year's concert and proceeded to dance with the performers.With official support, Jail Time Records has been able to flourish, offering opportunities to more prisoners, including those in New Bell's women's wing.Jeje, Jail Time Records first female artist, made her debut in 2022 with brooding Afrobeats song Show Me The Way."Nobody show me the way, nobody show me the way, I did it all alone," sings Jeje, who was jailed after stealing money and running away from an allegedly abusive uncle.As well as working with the women's wing, Jail Time Records have expanded their project outside New Bell and Cameroon. Roach and Happi set up a studio 1,000 miles (1,600km) away in 2023, in the central prison of Burkina Faso's capital city, Ouagadougou.Jail Time Records hopes it can replicate the success of the original New Bell studio, with its accompanying label, music video production arm and now, award-winning documentary.The film ends with an "in memoriam" sequence; a tribute to six prisoners who died while the Jail Time Records project has been running.New Bell may appear to be endlessly bleak, but according to Happi, music provides the inmates with a "lantern for a brighter future"."Before that, they had the stubborn mentality: it's them against the world," he says."They feel now important - they feel like they have a place in the society."

schema.headline: Jail Time Records: The notorious Cameroonian prison with its own record label

title: Rental searches for pet friendly properties drop after law change
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByCost of living correspondentRightmove searches for rental properties that allow pets have plummeted since law changes gave
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByCost of living correspondentRightmove searches for rental properties that allow pets have plummeted since law changes gave renters more rights.Following the introduction of the new rules, pet searches dropped by more than 50% in May and June compared with a year earlier.Landlords in England cannot unreasonably refuse pets in their properties under changes made in May in the Renters' Rights Act.But agents say some renters wrongly believe permission to have a pet is guaranteed, and landlords say some homes remain unsuitable for multiple pets or large dogs."Landlords must consider requests fairly and cannot unreasonably refuse them, but they can still decline where there is a valid reason," said Megan Eighteen, immediate past president of lettings agents trade body ARLA Propertymark.She said there was plenty of "potential for misunderstanding", among tenants about pet-friendly properties.Power shift over petsThe Rightmove data suggests that fewer tenants are proactively filtering for pet-friendly properties when searching for a home. While pets remain the most common searched-for term overall - ahead of gardens, garages and furnishings, the lead at the top is shrinking.Renter searches for properties that allow pets fell by 54% in May and 52% in June compared with the same months a year earlier, according to the figures shared with the BBC. Falls had accelerated through this year, as the changes got closer and were then introduced.Marc von Grundherr, director of agency Benham and Reeves, said some tenants have only disclosed a pet after signing their tenancy agreement, while others have been discovered during property inspections."The reality is that tenants now understand the balance of power has shifted. Landlords can no longer rely on a blanket 'no pets' policy to deter applications and should instead expect conversations around pet ownership to arise much later in the letting process," he said.Now, in England, landlords may still be able to refuse a pet if another tenant has an allergy, the property is too small for a large pet or several pets, the pet is illegal, or the landlord is a leaseholder and the freeholder does not allow pets.Before the rules changed, Eve Williamson had to give up her American Bulldog, Khan, or face eviction from her home - despite having previously had a dog in the property.The 41-year-old former hairdresser, from London, described the experience as awful, especially as Khan had brought comfort while she gave full-time care to her mum."Life can get tough, but pets bring unconditional love," she said. "They're family."Image source, Eve WilliamsonImage caption, Eve had to give up her dog - Khan - or face evictionKhan has since been happily re-homed, and Eve said she was delighted with the law change. Katie Smith, 29, from Swindon, has two cats - Pumpkin and Pippin - in her rental home. The new mum said the family had shared "wonderful moments" with pets, which would also teach children about life and death.But she said the choice of places to rent still dropped sharply on property portals when pets were part of the equation."Landlords should give them a chance," she said. Yet, even under the new rules, landlords were finding excuses to refuse potential tenants with pets, according to Russell Hunt, founder of Pets Lets, which matches clients with pet-friendly rentals.Image source, Russell HuntImage caption, Russell Hunt said landlords should consider each pet request on its meritsHe lives with a Basset Beagle cross, called Biscuit, and his three teenagers, who he jokes are more disruptive than the dog.He said pet CVs should be used and landlords should consider the circumstances more carefully, such as older dogs being calmer and sleeping more, rather than simply ruling out tenants with large or multiple pets. Cost to landlordsRepresentatives for landlords say they understand the importance of companionship that pets offer to tenants, but they can still face costly damage."Many landlords have legitimate concerns about the risk that some irresponsible pet owners pose to rental properties, or that some owners may try to keep pets in properties that are not appropriate for animals," said Chris Norris, chief policy officer at the National Residential Landlords Association.He said that landlords faced issues including: No power to compel tenants to take out insuranceNo legal right to request an additional depositA burden of costs should a pet cause damage to a propertyLesley Horton, the UK's chief property ombudsman said that landlords should not be levying pet surcharges as this fell outside permitted fees for issues such as late payments or lost key replacements.However, a landlord could make deductions from the tenancy deposit at the end of the tenancy for proven pet-related damage.Additional reporting by Kris Bramwell. Get in touchAre you affected by the issues raised in this story?

schema.headline: Rental searches for pet friendly properties drop after law change

title: Mr Motivator delivers fitness class at Huddersfield care home
description: Image source, Steve Jones/BBCImage caption, Mr Motivator rose to fame on our screens in the 1990sBySteve JonesYorkshireReporting fromLindleyTuesday af
body: Image source, Steve Jones/BBCImage caption, Mr Motivator rose to fame on our screens in the 1990sBySteve JonesYorkshireReporting fromLindleyTuesday afternoons at Lindley Park Care Home in Huddersfield are usually a time for relaxing, a short walk or enjoying something from the tea trolley as it makes it way round the peaceful 61-bed facility, which provides residential care and care for those with dementia.But today, it is party time.Mr Motivator, the 90s TV icon and original fitness influencer, is in town to deliver a fitness class to nine of the home's 42 residents.Lycra-clad and a kaleidoscope of colour, the 73-year-old moves like a man half his age as he leads a chairobics session soundtracked by a feel-good pop megamix."It's important when you get the opportunity to spread the message of wellbeing and movement that you grab it with both hands," he explains before the class."A care home is one of those places that needs the motivation."Image source, Steve Jones/BBCImage caption, Mr Motivator brightened up the day for residents at a care home in HuddersfieldMr Motivator's message has certainly landed in this quiet corner of West Yorkshire.Staff and residents follow along with moves like the steering wheel, air guitar and shooting the basketball.The room is full of bright colours and smiling faces, with ailments temporarily banished.In the corner, a visually impaired man gets up out of his chair to move his body and dance, much to the delight of staff."I have been doing this for 20 years and the one thing I've learned is that the last thing they want to be doing is sat around doing nowt," says one worker."They have all been doctors and nurses. It's us in 20 years."Despite spending four decades getting the nation moving, Mr Motivator insists he will "never" slow down.Figure caption, Mr Motivator puts care home residents through their paces"I meet too many people who retire and they are sitting around waiting to expire," he says."You don't know how much time you have been given, so therefore you need to try and ensure you are less dependent on other people."His message is that wellbeing is important to everyone, "it's just not enough of us embrace it"."The lines in the NHS could be half the size if everybody tomorrow took control of their own wellbeing - and that starts with wellbeing."Movement is medicine. Put a bit of laughter into it and it's even better medicine."According to the NHS, adults aged 65 and over should aim to be physically active every day and complete "at least 150 minutes of moderate intensity activity a week".Despite this, research from Sport England has found that 42% of people aged 55 and over are inactive, compared to 29% of the adult population.The afternoon's special visit has been organised by Bailey Greetham, who runs a business delivering fitness and wellbeing classes across the care sector.The 23-year-old, who was raised by his grandparents, says the idea to set up the business six years ago "sprung from a need for our older generation to move"."I realised the impact exercise has on our older generation and how important it is."Image source, Steve Jones/BBCImage caption, Bailey Greetham delivers fitness sessions for older adults across the countryBailey started his business in his hometown of Grimsby but he and his team now deliver fitness sessions acoss the country, including at Lindley Park."When you go into a care home and you see a resident you have been working with for weeks achieve something - stand for the first time, claim their independence back - it just puts it all into perspective."At the very least as long as we get people laughing and moving a little bit that's mission complete.""I enjoyed it very much," says Lindley Park resident Derek Wilson after the class."I had nothing else to do this afternoon, so it's been a pleasant change."Prior to arriving at the home David, a former industrial chemist who is originally from Bradford, lived in France for almost 20 years.His wife is still there trying to sell their house. So too are his five bikes, a nod to his love of cycling.Nowadays he uses a wheelchair, so is unable to ride.Image source, Steve Jones/BBCImage caption, Derek Wilson gave the class a thumbs upStill, today has provided some respite from the norm."I would like to be walking and standing but apart from that I'm alright," he says."Cycling was one of the original reasons why I went to France but unfortunately things were cut short because of my legs."I have to put up with it but I like what I have to put up with," he says of life at the care home back in Yorkshire.Elsewhere, 79-year-old Yvonne Noble, who now uses a wheelchair permanently after twice falling and breaking her legs, confesses the class has left her "ready for a cup of coffee".Image source, Steve Jones/BBCImage caption, Yvonne Noble was full of praise for Mr Motivator, even if she was a little tired"You have got to think positive when you do these things, you have got to put your heart into it," says Yvonne, a former accountant."I think he [Mr Motivator] is marvellous, I always did because I thought he can motivate people."Too many people don't try. You can do it."Image source, Judith Snell/BBCImage caption, Judith Snell was feeling the burn after the classSporting a bright pink headband, 84-year-old Judith Snell, from Brighouse, declares herself "ready for a punch-up" after completing some shadow boxing with Mr Motivator."My arms are a bit achey but I'm fine," she says."It was good. I'm glad I came."Get in touchYour Voice

schema.headline: Mr Motivator delivers fitness class at Huddersfield care home

title: What I learned when I reopened the Lockerbie bombing files
description: I thought the Lockerbie bombing was a closed case until I started asking questionsImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Officials inspect the wreck
body: I thought the Lockerbie bombing was a closed case until I started asking questionsImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Officials inspect the wreckage of Pan Am flight 103 on 21 December 1988ByMyles BonnarBBC DisclosureUpdated 57 minutes agoI was only a year old when the UK's deadliest terror attack shocked the world.In December 1988, Pan Am flight 103 exploded - killing all 259 people on board as well as 11 on the ground in the Scottish town of Lockerbie. I was a teenager by the time Libyan intelligence officer Abdelbaset al-Megrahi was convicted of the bombing in 2001 and, when he later died, I thought that was largely the end of the story.It wasn't. The case still rumbles on and, later this year, a man suspected of making the bomb which blew up the plane, Abu Agila Masud, goes on trial in Washington DC.As part of a Radio 4 Intrigue podcast series, I had an opportunity to delve into this complex case with fresh eyes.The deeper I dug, the more complicated Lockerbie became and there have been times that I don't know what to believe.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Abdelbaset al-Megrahi was the only man convicted of the Lockerbie bombingJim Swire, on the other hand, is sure what he believes - and it is not the official story.His daughter Flora died in the bombing, but he is convinced that whoever killed her got away with mass murder.Swire believes Megrahi is innocent, even befriending the convicted bomber up until his death in 2012."The burning issue was to get to the truth," he says."Always has been, always will be and I will not shut up about what I know to be true."Swire's doggedness has made him a prominent voice but most of the Lockerbie victims' families don't agree that Megrahi's conviction was a miscarriage of justice - and the bomber’s own appeals against the verdict either failed or were abandoned.For Swire, the simplest explanation is that Iran was behind the attack - not Libya.The Lockerbie bombing came five months after 290 people were killed when an Iranian commercial airliner was shot down by a US battleship.Iran swore revenge and months later Pan Am flight 103 exploded on its way to New York.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Jim Swire's daughter Flora died in the Lockerbie bombingAnd there's more.Iran - much like they do now - used proxy militant groups to pursue their ends.Before the Lockerbie bombing, a militant cell based in Frankfurt, part of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine - General Command (PFLP-GC), was foiled by German police.Police arrested suspects and seized explosive devices, concealed in radio cassette players, that were designed to trigger at altitude.The bomb that brought down Pan Am 103 was in a radio cassette player hidden inside a samsonite briefcase.Because of this, Swire believes the device that brought down Pan Am 103 was loaded at Frankfurt, and not Malta as the court had concluded.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, A mock-up of the explosives-loaded Toshiba cassette recorder which blew up Pan Am Flight 103And, for Swire, this is only the tip of the iceberg.He also questions much of the evidence presented at the 2001 trial, discredits witnesses, and is extremely suspicious of the involvement of intelligence agencies - like MI5, MI6 and the CIA - in the aftermath of the bombing.Combine these suspicions with his all-consuming grief and you can see why Swire is such a force to be reckoned with on his quest for a truth he believes has been denied to him."Discovering the truth became my way of handling the consequences of the grief reaction," Swire says."And it was very tough for other people to understand that but that's just the way I'm made, I suppose."Intrigue: LockerbieOn 21 December 1988, a plane explodes over Lockerbie, Scotland, killing 270 people. Almost four decades on, there's fresh evidence. Who was really behind the bombing?Dick Marquise, who led the FBI's Lockerbie task force, says that in the early days of the case he too believed the PFLP-GC were the "number one suspect", but years of investigation found nothing to prove it."There was not one shred of evidence that could be taken to court and get a conviction," he says. "You couldn't do it. There was nothing."However, there are others, besides Swire, who still question the "official narrative" - including former CIA agent John Holt who also believes Iran was behind the bombing.Holt worked with Libyan intelligence assets in the 1980s and was the handler of double agent Abdul Majid Giaka, whose information became central to the investigation into the Lockerbie bombing.Holt now believes Giaka was a "BS artist" who was out for money and was feeding the CIA fake stories to get paid."I didn't think much of him at all," he says."He gave us some little tidbits about what was going on, but he never knew anything about the Pan Am bombing. And he knew a lot about Megrahi," Holt says.Holt believes the fact the CIA bankrolled Giaka devalues him as an informant."It makes it easier for somebody to say whatever the person who's giving them money wants them to say," Holt says.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Members of the armed forces collect debris from residential gardens after the mid-air explosion of Pan Am Flight 103I managed to get a hold of the CIA papers - known as cables - from the time, which showed what Giaka had told the Americans.The cables date back to the months before Lockerbie and include notes of conversations between Giaka and Holt and two earlier CIA handlers.Within the cables, Giaka places Megrahi in Malta - where the bomb was said to have been planted - at a key time in the Lockerbie plot.Megrahi is also said to have visited a Maltese clothes shop, buying shirts and baby grows - which were placed in the suitcase with the bomb and later found at the plane crash site.Giaka had even talked to the CIA about eight kilos of orange-coloured explosives stored at the Malta airport offices. Semtex, the explosive used in Lockerbie, is orange.In the 2001 trial, Giaka was to be a "key" witness in the prosecution's case but the four judges de­scribed some of his evidence as "at best grossly ex­ag­ger­ated and at worst sim­ply un­true".The Senussi filesDecades on from Megrahi's conviction, new intelligence documents have been recovered allegedly from the heart of Libyan intelligence.They are believed to have come from Libyan leader Colonel Gaddafi's notorious intelligence network run by his spy chief Abdullah Senussi.These leaked Libyan intelligence documents contain information that could potentially put an end to the doubt, theories and countertheories that have tied so many, including me, in knots.The original 'Senussi Files', as they are now known, were shown to French journalists who later published a book, The Murderer Who Must Be Saved.I travelled to Paris to meet one of the authors, investigative journalist Vincent Nouzille.He brought piles of documents, enough to cover the whole bed and the hotel room desk.You can tell he loves his work and despite having pored over these documents for years, he's still awestruck by their content.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Lockerbie bombing accused Lamin Khalif Fhimah (left) with Libyan leader Colonel Gaddafi after his acquittal in 2001Some of the Senussi files date back to autumn 1988, in the months before Lockerbie, and contain documents apparently detailing plans to target aircraft on multi-stop flights using a 11-hour long-delay timer bomb concealed in luggage much like the Lockerbie bombing.It even mentions tests on concealing a device inside a tape recorder.As we go through each document, my head is spinning.There are references to dry runs, apparent weaknesses in airport security, and enough detail about the movements of Megrahi and others for Nouzille to crosscheck dates and places against other sources.Nouzille says he spent three years carefully verifying everything in the files.He shows me another file which details the apparent movements of Megrahi and Masud, coming in and out of Malta.This account lines up with the information provided in the CIA cables from the previously discredited Giaka."We know from the CIA cables that Giaka reported the same people, the same dates, the same false passport, at the same date," Nouzille says."So two sources, independent, which match."Image source, ReutersImage caption, Abu Agila Masud is accused of making the bomb that blew up Pan Am flight 103 The Senussi Files seem to corroborate several details first mentioned in the cables, including the presence of semtex at Luqa Airport in Malta.Nouzille shows me a translated document, signed by Megrahi, dated January 87, which mentions "10 kilos of explosive material" stored at the airport by Lamin Khalif Fhimah, the man who stood trial alongside Megrahi in 2001 but was acquitted.I tried to contact Fhimah via his trial lawyer to put these allegations to him, but I was unable to reach him.Nouzille concedes that these documents are not "final proof" that Libya was targeting Pan Am 103 flight, but he believes this is evidence of their modus operandi."We have a preparation of a multi-stop flight and a suitcase - and after 11 hours the bomb will explode," Nouzille says.The Senussi Files that Nouzille has are copies, not originals, so they cannot be forensically tested.It remains to be seen whether they will be admissible in the upcoming trial.If they're authentic, these files may prove once and for all that Megrahi was guilty.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Paul Hudson, whose daughter Melina was one of the victims, holds up a banner outside the federal court in Washington DCAs Nouzille packed away the documents, I thought of Jim Swire and what this could all mean for him.He's devoted his life to this case - even befriending Megrahi during his quest to find answers.However, despite the years spent by Nouzille to authenticate the documents, the Senussi Files have failed to convince him that Libya was responsible.Swire says: "I don't think that you should, with your eyes open, go into believing that any documents, however perfect they may seem to be, are genuine which prove conveniently that this was a Libyan job."He said the CIA had the ability to forge any documents they wanted.Despite several delays, Masud is due to go on trial in August this year.Whether this will be pushed back again remains to be seen.It's very likely that historical evidence from the original Lockerbie trial will be brought under the microscope once again - opening up old wounds and catalysing a new era of questioning.Or, if admissible and verified, the Senussi Files might prove once and for all what Dick Marquise and other investigators have been saying all along.

schema.headline: What I learned when I reopened the Lockerbie bombing files

body: Depending on the contract you have, data charges may apply for accessing the internet on your mobile device.If you are not sure about the potential charges, please ask your mobile network provider. You may find some costs are included in your existing price plan or that you can opt for a data package that gives reduced charges for accessing the internet.The BBC does not charge you to access mobile content.
